methodological_rigor.justification: Nationwide population-based cancer registry analysis using all German cancer registries (population ~83 million) covering 2009-2023 with 2025 NEN cases, making this one of the largest cohorts for this rare tumor. Methods use ICD-10/ICD-O-3 coding, joinpoint regression for incidence trends, age-standardized incidence with old European standard, period analysis for 5-year relative survival per Brenner methodology, and multiple imputation to handle missing AJCC stage. Appropriate sensitivity analyses and complete-case vs imputation comparisons are presented. Limitations (misclassification, missing subtype/grading, excluded registries) are candidly discussed. Small subgroup (NET-G3 n=9.0% survival based on few events) leads to imprecise estimates, which authors acknowledge.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is a large population-based cohort study (retrospective registry) which maps to Oxford LoE 2b. The findings have direct clinical and guideline-relevant implications: the WHO G1-G3 grading of esophageal NETs is shown to carry strong prognostic information (5-year RS 83.8%, 50.0%, 9.0% respectively), supporting the validity of the grading system. NEC/MiNEN prognosis is worse than AC/SCC, informing patient counseling. The study fills a gap explicitly noted in the 2019 WHO classification where grading impact could not be assessed due to limited data.

reporting_quality.justification: As an observational registry cohort study, STROBE is applicable. Key STROBE items are well addressed: clear setting (Germany-wide registries), data sources (Robert Koch Institute), case definitions via explicit ICD-O-3 codes, statistical methods (ASRs, joinpoint, period analysis, multiple imputation with supplementary statistical details), participant numbers, and discussion of limitations including misclassification and excluded registries. Supplementary materials are referenced for imputation details, absolute survival, and AC/SCC comparators. Data availability is limited: registry data is not publicly shareable (common constraint), and no code is released.

novelty_literature.justification: SEER-based analyses of esophageal NECs have been published (Li 2020, Chen 2022, Lin 2023, Yang 2025 cited). The present work's distinctive contribution is the largest population-based cohort specifically addressing NET G1-G3 grading prognosis in the esophagus, which the WHO classification explicitly said could not be assessed. The comparisons with AC/SCC from identical methodology and the EGJ vs esophagus differences are incremental but meaningfully extend prior work. Not first-in-class, but a solid gap-filling contribution.

writing_presentation.justification: Well-organized manuscript with clear structure, precise epidemiological vocabulary, and careful presentation of results with 95% CIs for key comparisons. Tables and figures are appropriately referenced. Limitations are discussed transparently. Occasional minor issues (e.g., one line 'Since multiple physicians are often involved... there are at least three types of reporting sources') but overall publication-ready prose with appropriate statistical framing (authors explicitly note they focus on precision over significance testing).

key_strengths: Largest population-based cohort (n=2025) of esophageal/EGJ NENs analyzed with nationwide German registry data, directly addressing a gap noted in the 2019 WHO classification
Rigorous epidemiological methods: joinpoint regression, age-standardization, period analysis per Brenner, multiple imputation for missing AJCC stage
Clear clinical message: WHO G1-G3 NET grading has strong prognostic effect (5-year RS 83.8% vs 50.0% vs 9.0%), supporting validity of the grading system
Transparent handling of limitations including misclassification, missing data, and excluded registries
Appropriate inclusion of AC/SCC comparators using identical methodology
key_concerns: NET-G3 subgroup is small, leading to imprecise survival estimates; authors acknowledge
Missing NEC subtyping (45%) and missing AJCC staging limit some analyses despite imputation
Retrospective registry design cannot address treatment effects or biological mechanisms
Cannot fully distinguish true incidence trend from improved reporting/coding over time
No public data or code sharing (registry constraint)
chief_reviewer.rationale: Solid, well-executed population-based epidemiology on a rare tumor with clear guideline-relevant findings. Fits Tier 3 with minor revisions.
